source: Tarabeih (2026) Prospect Theory in Large Language Models: A Meta-Analysis of Loss Aversion, Diminishing Sensitivity, and Probability Weighting
finding: Across 11 studies and 32 models, LLMs show modest loss aversion, near-linear value functions under one fitting method, and a human-like inverse-S probability weighting. The average hides huge differences between models.
numbers: 102 fitted estimates (28 loss aversion, 43 curvature, 31 weighting). Pooled lambda 1.26 (95% CI 1.06-1.46); human meta-analyses 1.07, 1.31, 1.96. Prediction interval for lambda 0.20-2.31. Curvature 1.01 (Tversky-Kahneman fit, human 0.67) vs 0.52 (Tanaka fit, human 0.67). Weighting gamma 0.81 (TK) and 0.84 (Tanaka).
quote: Loss aversion is modest: the pooled lambda is 1.26, far below the strongest human meta-analytic estimate (1.96)
limits: Few studies per cell; standard errors mostly imputed; fitting methods differ; 6 boundary-edge fits excluded; abstract screening done by an LLM (84% agreement with author, kappa 0.49).
agent_relevance: Do not assume a model has a fixed prospect-theory profile. Measure the specific model, or avoid relying on it.

source: Tarabeih (2026) meta-analysis: design moderators
finding: Loss aversion in LLMs matches people when gains and losses are symmetric but is far below people when losses are smaller than gains (the design where human loss aversion is strongest). Newer models are less loss averse.
numbers: Symmetric designs (18 estimates, 7 studies): lambda 1.15 [0.98,1.32] vs human 1.07. Losses < gains (10 estimates, 4 studies): 1.46 [0.96,1.96] vs human about 2.3 (p=.004). Model family R2=.27; Gemini about +0.69 over GPT; lambda falls about 0.16 per release year; +0.35 per tenfold stake increase (p=.030). GPT-3.5 2.72 to GPT-4.1 0.57. Persona conditioning not significant.
limits: Family and year effects rest on few studies (10 studies; cluster-robust tests weak); stake effect not significant alone.
agent_relevance: Newer, more capable models drift toward expected-value behaviour, so a scaffold cannot count on human-like loss aversion being present.

source: Tarabeih (2026) meta-analysis: supplementary S1 on Yechiam & Tarabeih
finding: A model's measured loss aversion depends on what literature it has just read; the author calls the parameter a response drawn out by the prompt rather than a fixed preference.
numbers: Given Brown et al. (2024) (strong loss aversion) models were loss averse; given Yechiam & Zeif (2025) lambda 1.0-1.1, near baselines 1.05 and 1.09.
limits: Summary of a study the meta-analyst co-authored.
agent_relevance: Context in the prompt can set the bias. Neutral framing of instructions matters.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in LLMs
finding: Five LLMs (GPT-4o, o3, Claude Sonnet 4 with and without thinking, Gemini 1.5 Pro) showed gain/loss framing effects in some scenarios but not others. Direction and size depended on scenario wording, not on the math.
numbers: Three-option scenarios with equal expected value; 750 civilian decisions plus geopolitical ones. Championship strategy: 85.6% risky BLITZ in loss frame vs 0.8% in gain frame (88.8% safe CONTROL). Career transition reversed: 87.2% safe APPLY in loss frame vs 41.6% in gain frame. Business merger: 65.6% vs 62.4% accept (no effect). Framing effect not correlated with how often models computed expected value.
limits: Single author; novel scenarios without a human control group; Gemini 2.5 Pro excluded for refusals; Mann-Whitney tests per scenario.
agent_relevance: Framing bias is a property of the words in a problem. A scaffold that restates a problem neutrally may reduce it.

source: Payne (2025) math control experiment
finding: When the same structure was given as pure symbols, GPT-4o and o3 showed no framing effect at all and chose indifference.
numbers: Indifference in 100% of cases in both gain and loss frames; o3 treated value as linear and computed EV 0.5 for all three options. 400 mathematical trials.
limits: Only two models tested; indifference is a forced reading of equal EV, so it is a weak test of risk attitude.
agent_relevance: Translating a problem into explicit symbols and expected values removes the framing effect: a cheap scaffold move.

source: Wang, Lin, Liu et al. (2025/2026) Rethinking Prospect Theory for LLMs (MarPT)
finding: Prospect theory does not describe all LLMs. Small models fit poorly, and fitted parameters drift when numeric probabilities are replaced by verbal markers like 'likely'.
numbers: Tanaka 35 lottery pairs, 256 samples each (8,960 choices per condition). Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B failed the fit criteria (MAE > 0.20 and McFadden R2 < 0.10). Human baseline 0.670 / 2.630 / 0.685. Fits: Qwen2.5-32B 0.598/1.213/0.867; GPT-5-Mini 0.447/4.000/2.888; Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.495/1.499/0.814 (column order assumed curvature, loss aversion, weighting). Temperature 0.7; reasoning disabled for open models.
quote: PT does not consistently provide a reliable account of LLM decision-making across models
limits: Column labels read from a garbled table; human baseline from Tanaka et al. 2010; closed models constrained against explicit EV calculation; 14 verbal markers.
agent_relevance: Verbal uncertainty (as in real agent loops) changes behaviour that numeric tests would not predict. Test with the wording the agent will meet.

source: Jia, Yuan, Pan, McNamara, Chen (2024) Decision-making behavior evaluation framework for LLMs under uncertain context
finding: Three commercial LLMs were risk averse and loss averse with small-probability overweighting, but differed a lot among themselves. Demographic personas shifted parameters.
numbers: 300 repeated multiple-price-list runs per model (GPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-1.0-Pro). All three had mean risk aversion above 0. GPT-4-Turbo weighting parameter about 1.18 (diverges from human norm) and lowest loss concern (about 1.48 mean). Claude riskier overall but higher loss aversion. Personas (sexual minority, disability) made Claude more risk averse.
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction, so only text-stated results kept; old model versions.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts shift risk attitude in ways that raise fairness questions; avoid unneeded personas in a decision scaffold.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) LLM economicus? Mapping the behavioral biases of LLMs via utility theory
finding: Fitted utility functions to GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo and others. Results were neither fully human-like nor fully rational: weaker loss aversion, similar risk aversion, stronger time discounting than people.
numbers: Gamble games M=56 settings, N=100 samples at temperature 1. GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo showed no probability distortion for gains. GPT-4 Turbo overweighted low and underweighted high probabilities for losses. GPT-4 risk averse for losses; GPT-4 Turbo risk seeking for losses like humans. Models also included GPT-3.5, Llama 2 (7B/13B/70B), Mistral 7B, Gemini 1.0 Pro, Claude 2.1; Claude 2.1 failed the competence test for risk and loss.
limits: Competence test excluded some models; human values taken from classic studies, not matched samples.
agent_relevance: Model behaviour on risky choice is inconsistent even inside one family.

source: Ross, Kim, Lo (2024) prompting interventions on GPT-4 risk and loss aversion
finding: Telling GPT-4 to be risk or loss averse barely worked, and zero-shot chain of thought did not move it toward rationality. One example in the prompt worked; two examples confused it.
numbers: Direct prompt: value function only slightly shifted for gains; for losses it became more concave instead of the expected convex. Zero-shot CoT: no substantial change. One-shot: successful shift. Two-shot: gain and loss examples confounded, weaker or no shift. N=10 samples per setting over 56 settings. Role-playing a teenager or senior: less loss averse; giving advice to the same ages gave different shifts.
limits: Single model (GPT-4); N=10 per setting; figures not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Naming a bias in the prompt is a weak lever; examples work better. Roleplay and advice modes differ, so test the mode the agent uses.

source: Hartley et al. (2025) How personality traits shape LLM risk-taking behaviour
finding: GPT-4o acted as a risk-neutral rational agent on non-mixed prospects: its certainty equivalents matched expected values. Big Five prompts, mainly Openness, shifted risk parameters as in humans, but could not make it risk seeking for gains.
numbers: Certainty equivalents for GPT-4o near indistinguishable from a risk-neutral agent; Openness correlation with risk taking for gains 0.63, with risk aversion for losses 0.44. GPT-4-Turbo generalised the personality-risk link inconsistently. GPT-4o scored above human averages on Conscientiousness and Agreeableness.
limits: Only GPT-4o and GPT-4-Turbo; CPT fit on small prospect datasets.
agent_relevance: A newer model can be near expected value by default, so a scaffold built for human-like bias may have no effect.

source: Chen, Liu, Shan, Zhong (2023) The emergence of economic rationality of GPT
finding: GPT made budget decisions that largely satisfied utility maximisation, with higher rationality scores than human subjects. It was sensitive to language frames of the choice situation.
numbers: Abstract only: four domains (risk, time, social, food); rationality score via revealed preference; lower heterogeneity than humans.
limits: Abstract read, not full paper.
agent_relevance: Rationality rises with newer models, but wording still moves choices.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci) was run on Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 problem pairs and showed three of six biases: framing, certainty effect and overweighting of small-probability differences.
numbers: Over 13,000 choice problems; only the largest GPT-3 model solved them above chance (t(29134) = -16.85) but below humans (t(29134) = -11.50). Three biases not found: the other three of the six identified by K&T.
limits: GPT-3 only (2022); biases inferred from choice probabilities; later models differ.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that text training imports prospect-style biases.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT showed the gain/loss framing effect and the endowment effect like people.
numbers: Framing: ChatGPT rated medicine efficacy 5 in all 11 positive-frame trials and 4 in all 11 negative-frame trials; humans 5.2 vs 4.6 (t(80)=3.86, p<0.001). Endowment: kept the 2-year-old coin in 37 of 40 trials (92.5%, CI 79.6-98.4); humans 34 of 40 (85%).
limits: Rating-scale framing, not monetary gamble choices; one model; the authors had to avoid money vignettes.
agent_relevance: Framing carries through non-monetary language, which matches Payne's finding that language drives it.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Framework with 13,465 prompts to test cognitive bias in LLM decisions and mitigation, including self-help where the model rewrites its own prompt.
numbers: Abstract: 13,465 prompts; prompt-induced, sequential and inherent bias categories.
limits: Abstract only; prospect-theory-specific numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Self-debiasing prompts exist; compare with the debiasing subfield.

source: Ge, Zhang, Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) gap: risky choices of reasoning vs conversational LLMs
finding: 20 LLMs split into reasoning models (near expected value, insensitive to framing and order) and conversational models (less rational, sensitive to framing, ordering and explanation). Maths training is the key difference.
numbers: Correlation with risk-neutral economicus: reasoning models 0.86 to 1; conversational models below 0.5; humans near 0. Highest LLM-human correlation 0.42 (Claude Haiku). Reasoning models nearly order-invariant and frame-invariant; humans less framing-sensitive than conversational models. All models show a description-history gap. Temperature 1; matched Prolific human experiment.
quote: RMs tend towards rational behavior, are insensitive to the order of prospects, gain/loss framing, and explanations
limits: Three base prospect pairs only; prospect-theory parameters not directly estimated.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode removes framing bias but also removes human-likeness; choose by purpose.

source: Ge et al. (2026) DH gap: explanation effects
finding: Asking for a rationale changes choices. Brief explanations made models more rational than no explanation or mathematical explanations. Longer rationales sometimes reduced rationality.
numbers: Qualitative from text: brief explanation closer to economicus; math explanations no better; effect larger for conversational models.
limits: Exact effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Requiring a rationale is not neutral: test it per model before adding to an agent loop.

source: Liu, Gu, Griffiths et al. (2024) Large language models assume people are more rational than we really are
finding: On the choices13k human gambling data, LLMs predicted and simulated choices closer to expected value than to people.
numbers: GPT-4o Spearman 0.94 with max-EV choice versus 0.48 for humans. CoT simulation 0.90 for GPT-4o. In the zero-shot test against real human choices, GPT-4-Turbo and GPT-4o correlated 0.41 and 0.28 with max EV (as read).
limits: Fine-grained numbers partly ambiguous in extraction; description-based gambles only; author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Using an LLM as a stand-in for human risky choice will overstate rationality.

source: Yechiam & Tarabeih (2026) Mimicry without understanding: the origins of decision bias in LLMs
finding: ChatGPT-4o and Qwen showed loss aversion when told about human loss aversion. The loss aversion level reported in a paper predicted the model's own level.
numbers: ChatGPT lambda: 1.09 baseline; 1.785 after Brown et al. abstract (strong loss aversion); 1.043 after Yechiam & Zeif (none); 1.52 after the full Brown report. ChatGPT accepted 105% more lotteries after Yechiam & Zeif than after Brown; Qwen 9% gap. Qwen lambda 1.170 vs 1.047. Regression McFadden r2=.58.
quote: Scientific papers of biases can thus become self-fulfilling prophecies
limits: Two models; stylised lotteries.
agent_relevance: Bias literature in context can self-fulfil. Keep bias descriptions out of the working context unless wanted.

source: Dubedy (2026) Persona-conditioned risk behavior in LLMs: simulated gambling with GPT-4.1
finding: GPT-4.1 given a Rich, Middle or Poor persona played very different numbers of slot-machine rounds, matching reference-dependent risk taking without being told about prospect theory.
numbers: 50 iterations per condition, 6,950 decisions. Mean rounds: Poor 37.39 (SD 15.5), Middle 7.83, Rich 1.11. Kruskal-Wallis H=393.5; Cohen's d=4.15 Poor vs Rich on risk score. Emotion labels looked post hoc; belief updating negligible (rho=0.032).
limits: Independent single-author, one model, persona confounded with plain instruction compliance (the Rich persona stops).
agent_relevance: Persona sets a reference point in an agent; could drive behaviour strongly.

source: Du (2025) Mitigating gambling-like risk-taking behaviors in LLMs (RARG)
finding: Proposes a training framework with a loss-aversion mechanism to cut gambling-like behaviour in LLMs.
numbers: Reported: 18.7% reduction in overconfidence bias, 24.3% reduction in loss-chasing; 52.4% reduction on a loss-chasing detection measure. Attention separability 2.3x.
limits: Single-author preprint; methods vague; no independent replication; training-based, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Low evidence weight. Idea only: penalise escalation after losses.

source: Ethayarajh, Xu, Muennighoff, Jurafsky, Kiela (2024) KTO: model alignment as prospect theoretic optimization
finding: Uses the Kahneman-Tversky value function with a reference point and a loss-aversion weight as the training objective for aligning LLMs from binary feedback. It matches or beats DPO at 1B-30B.
numbers: Works with 90% of the desirable data discarded and still beats DPO. Swapping DPO for KTO on Zephyr-SFT raised GSM8K by 13.5 points. Ablation (MMLU/GSM8k/HumanEval/BBH): KTO default 58.6/53.5/30.9/52.6; risk-neutral value function 57.3/42.0/28.8/6.1; concave log value 58.3/42.5/30.6/43.2. Loss aversion weights D, U default 1.
limits: Prospect theory borrowed for the loss shape, not as a human claim; gains partly come from not needing paired data; DPO ties on Pythia.
agent_relevance: Shows a prospect-theory shape is a useful tool inside training. Not a scaffold item.

source: Wang, Lin, Liu et al. (2025/2026) MarPT: scale and stability
finding: Larger LLMs fit prospect theory better and are more stable under verbal uncertainty, but loss aversion stays unstable and small models drift to boundary values.
numbers: Marker-to-probability mappings keep their order across models ('almost certain' about 95%, 'doubtful' about 20% in the mapping table) but absolute values differ by model. Mistral-7B parameters swing and hit boundary values.
limits: Conclusion limited to the 35-lottery Tanaka design; no matched humans.
agent_relevance: Models treat 'likely' differently from each other; do not mix verbal confidence with numeric reasoning without calibration.

source: Han et al. (2026) Reproducing human biases in route choice using LLMs
finding: 3,000 LLM agents with occupation, risk preference and travel purpose profiles chose routes. The authors report behaviour consistent with cumulative prospect theory, with reference points inferred by the LLM.
numbers: 3,000 agents; reference point inferred from expected travel time; gain and loss domains built from time distributions (45-minute limit).
limits: Summary-level; no per-parameter numbers extracted; no human control seen in this read.
agent_relevance: LLM-inferred reference points is one use of the method inside an agent simulation.

source: Niimi (2025) Reference points in LLM sentiment analysis
finding: Supplying reference points (prior rating, expectations) as structured JSON input improved sentiment prediction for a 3B model.
numbers: Macro-F1 up 1.6% and 4%; RMSE down 16% and 9.1% on Yelp Restaurant and Nightlife. Follow-up says gains are genuine contextual reasoning, not label proxying.
limits: One small model; marketing text; prospect theory only motivates the design.
agent_relevance: Reference-point framing works as a prompt format for small models.

source: Hans, Gurney, Marsella, Hirschmann (2025) Quantifying loss aversion in cyber adversaries via LLM analysis
finding: LLMs segmented hacker notes into actions and linked persistence mechanisms to triggers to extract loss-aversion signals from real human behaviour.
numbers: Hackers in a controlled demo network; qualitative. No effect size read.
limits: Conference paper; no ground truth for loss aversion; small sample.
agent_relevance: Uses an LLM as a coder of loss-aversion evidence, not as the decision maker.

source: Horton (2023) Large language models as simulated economic agents: Homo silicus
finding: Replicated Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler (1986) fairness and related experiments with GPT-3 and found results qualitatively like the originals.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract read, not full paper.
agent_relevance: Early line of work treating LLMs as simulated participants.

source: Binz et al. (2025) Centaur: a foundation model of human cognition
finding: Fine-tuning an LLM on Psych-101 (160 experiments, over 60,000 participants, 10 million choices) gives a model that predicts held-out human choices better than cognitive models.
numbers: Abstract only: 160 experiments, 60,000+ participants, 10,000,000+ choices.
limits: Abstract only; fit on prospect-theory tasks not checked.
agent_relevance: If human-like risky choice is wanted, fine-tuning beats prompting; not available to a scaffold.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1992) Advances in prospect theory (benchmark values used by LLM papers)
finding: Human benchmark for cumulative prospect theory used by the LLM studies above: curvature about 0.88, lambda about 2.25, weighting about 0.61 (gains) and 0.69 (losses).
numbers: Values quoted from memory of the 1992 paper; the meta-analysis uses human curvature 0.67 and lambda 1.07-1.96 instead.
limits: Not opened; human values are disputed (lambda from 1.07 to 1.96 across three recent meta-analyses).
agent_relevance: The human reference is itself uncertain, so 'human-like' is a moving target.
